# Rāhula Saṁyutta (SN 18)

**ID:** SN 18  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Rāhula Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul6.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul6.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Rāhula Saṁyutta* (SN 18; also spelled *Rāhulasaṁyutta*), titled the "Linked Discourses with Rāhula," is the eighteenth collection of the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003]. Set at Jeta's Grove near Sāvatthī, the collection opens with the Venerable Rāhula—the son of the Buddha, who was ordained as a novice during the Buddha's first return to Kapilavatthu—approaching the Buddha to ask for a concise Dhamma teaching so that he might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, and ardent [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x]. The samyutta comprises twenty-two short discourses arranged in two chapters (*vagga*s) [Bodhi 2003]. While classified under the programmatic heading of a "Specific Person," the text provides virtually no personal or narrative detail, functioning instead as a strictly doctrinal exposition focused on the three characteristics of impermanence (*anicca*), suffering (*dukkha*), and non-self (*anattā*) [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x].

Throughout the collection, the Buddha interrogates Rāhula across fifty-nine doctrinal categories [Kuznetsova et al. 2012; Williams, Critical Concepts]. These encompass the six internal sense bases and six external sense objects, followed by six classes each of consciousness (*viññāṇa*), contact (*samphassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*sañcetanā*), and craving (*taṇhā*), as well as the six elements (*dhātu*) and the five aggregates (*khandha*) [Williams, Critical Concepts]. Early discourses enumerate consecutive pentads of mental factors (*phassa-pañcamā*) [Nyanaponika and Bodhi 2012]. Applying the standard catechetical formula to these categories demonstrates that conditioned phenomena are not fit to be regarded as "mine," "I am," or "myself," thereby leading the practitioner to revulsion (*nibbidā*), dispassion (*virāga*), and liberation (*vimutti*) [Bodhi 2003_x; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka].
